summary: Discusses the threats to protocols that carry authentication for network access and the security requirements that follow, as input for the PANA working group's design.

eli5.summary: Before building a lock for a door, you think about the ways burglars could get in. This is that list for network login.

questions: what is a bidding down attack
subtitle: The attacks a network-access login protocol must survive, and the eight requirements that follow.

tldr.problem: A device that wants network access has no prior trust with the network's authentication agent, and attackers on a shared link can spoof, replay, hijack or steal service.
tldr.mechanism: The memo goes through each stage (discovery, authentication, leaving, service use, agent to enforcement point traffic) and lists the threats, with when they apply to shared and non-shared links, and derives eight requirements.
tldr.outcome: The requirements, such as mutual authentication, key establishment and protected disconnect messages, were written as input for the PANA working group's protocol design.

facts.label: Threat stages
facts.value: Discovery, authentication, leaving, service theft, PAA-EP, miscellaneous

today: RFC 4016 is an Informational memo and, according to its metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It was written as input to the PANA working group's protocol design.

sections.title: Purpose and Terminology
sections.content:
The Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access (PANA) working group is developing IP-based methods for authenticating clients to an access network. A client must discover the address of the PANA authentication agent (PAA), run an authentication protocol, and may exchange more messages during its network access. This memo discusses the threats at these steps without discussing solutions, and its requirements go to the working group as input.

Key roles are the PANA Client (PaC), the PAA, the Authentication Server (AS), the Enforcement Point (EP) that filters packets, and the Device Identifier (DI) used to control a client's access, which may contain an IP address, link-layer address or switch port number. At most one PaC should be associated with a DI on a PAA.
sections.eli5: Someone who wants to join a network has to prove who they are to a gatekeeper. This memo lists what could go wrong before the gate is designed.

sections.title: Usage Scenarios and Trust
sections.content:
PANA is meant for places with no prior trust or security association between the PaC and other nodes such as the PAA and EP. The link may be shared (Ethernet) or not (DSL). Even if all PaCs are authenticated at layer 2, they still do not trust each other, and any PaC can pretend to be a PAA or spoof IP addresses.

Some pairs do trust each other beforehand. The PAA and AS are protected by a security association, with those threats already covered in RFC 3579. The PAA and EP share an administrative domain, and the PaC and AS share a home domain. The PaC and PAA, and the PaC and EP, have no prior trust. A security association is built during authentication, and keys can then secure the link between the PaC and EP.
sections.eli5: Some helpers already know each other, like the gatekeeper and the office behind them. The visitor knows nobody at first, so everything the visitor says to the gatekeeper has to be treated carefully.

sections.title: Threats in Discovery, Authentication and Leaving
sections.content:
A malicious node can send a spoofed advertisement and pretend to be the PAA. Because advertisements can carry supported authentication methods, it can also cause a bidding down attack, which tricks the PaC into a weaker method. Discovery is hard to protect without prior trust, so PANA must not assume it is protected.

During authentication, an attacker can send false success or failure indications, mount a man-in-the-middle attack (particularly with compound methods that are not cryptographically bound), replay earlier messages, or exploit the device identifier. In the device identifier attack, an attacker relays the real client's authentication and then gets access under its own IP or MAC address.

When a client leaves, a node can pretend to be the PAA and revoke access, pretend to be the PaC and send a disconnect, or take over after a client leaves silently, for example when a cable is unplugged. For most of these, the memo says the threat is absent on a non-shared link, because ingress filtering stops impersonation, and present on a shared link even when layer 2 offers some protection.
sections.eli5: A trickster can pretend to be the gatekeeper, say 'you passed' or 'you failed' falsely, repeat old messages, or slip in after you walk away. These tricks mostly work when many people share the same hallway.

sections.title: Service Theft, Agent Traffic and Other Attacks
sections.content:
After authentication the EP filters packets using something on every packet, such as IP and MAC addresses. An attacker who sniffs those addresses can spoof both and use the network for free. Binding the session to the device identifier and bootstrapping a shared secret between the PaC and PAA lets a security association be set up between the PaC and EP.

The PAA passes access control information, at least the device identifier, to the EP. An eavesdropper could learn it, or an attacker pretending to be the PAA could send false information. Protecting that traffic removes both threats.

Miscellaneous denial of service attacks are noted. An attacker can flood the PAA with authentication requests so it uses memory for state, or force expensive computation on the PAA or AS. If IP addresses are assigned before authentication, attackers can deplete the address space or answer every duplicate address detection query. The memo says that fixing only address depletion would not improve overall security, and that secure address resolution such as SEND can prevent the DAD attack. It also says the link should be assumed to be shared for most threats.
sections.eli5: If a thief copies your pass number, they can walk in as you. The fix is to tie your entry to a secret that only you and the gatekeeper share, and to keep the gatekeeper's notes to the guard private.

sections.title: The Eight Requirements
sections.content:
The memo's summary lists eight requirements. Where the wording is 'PANA MUST be able to', the protocol must be capable of the protection, and a deployment may or may not use it.

  • PANA MUST NOT assume the discovery process is protected.
  • PANA MUST be able to mutually authenticate the PaC and PAA and establish keys to protect PANA messages.
  • Compound authentication methods MUST be cryptographically bound.
  • PANA MUST be able to protect itself against replay attacks.
  • PANA MUST be able to protect the device identifier against spoofing when exchanged between the PaC and PAA.
  • PANA MUST be able to protect disconnect and revocation messages, and MUST NOT depend on the PaC sending a disconnect message.
  • PANA MUST securely bind the authenticated session to the device identifier and be able to bootstrap a shared secret for the PaC to EP security association.
  • PAA to EP communication MUST be protected against eavesdropping and spoofing.
sections.eli5: The rules say: do not trust the first hello, prove who each side is, tie the pass to the person, ignore repeated old messages, and keep the gatekeeper's notes private.

viz.caption: THREAT AREAS AND THE REQUIREMENT NUMBERS THAT ANSWER THEM

items.title: Discovery
items.text: Spoofed advertisements and bidding down. Requirement 1.

items.title: Authentication
items.text: False indications, MITM, replay, device identifier. Requirements 2 to 5.

items.title: Leaving
items.text: Fake disconnects and silent departures. Requirement 6.

items.title: Service theft
items.text: Spoofed IP and MAC addresses. Requirement 7.

items.title: PAA to EP
items.text: Eavesdropping and spoofed access information. Requirement 8.
